hints: Focus on the shape of the graph, especially the very large fall between two consecutive elements, as this tells you where a new period starts.
The high point just before the big drop is a noble gas with a very stable electron configuration, so the next low point starts Group 1 of the next period.
Work backwards one place from the noble gas to find the Group 17 element, then recall which group forms simple covalent hydrides of type HX.
walkthrough:
**Read the pattern in ionisation energy**

Look for the most dramatic feature. There is a small rise from A to B, then a huge fall from B to C, then a small rise from C to D.

In ionisation energy trends, a huge fall always means we have just finished one period and started a new shell.

**Assign the groups to B and C**

The element before the big drop, B, must have a very high first ionisation energy. That fits a noble gas, Group 18, with a stable full outer shell.

The element after the big drop, C, must have a very low first ionisation energy. That fits an alkali metal, Group 1, where the outer electron is in a new shell, far from the nucleus and well shielded:
$$\text{B (high IE) = Group 18, C (low IE) = Group 1}$$

**Work out A and D and link to HX**

Because atomic numbers are consecutive, A is one proton before B, so A is Group 17, a halogen. D is one proton after C, so D is Group 2.

Only a halogen (Group 17) reacts with hydrogen to give a simple covalent molecule $\text{HX}$, such as $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ or $\text{HF}$. Therefore X must be element A.

options.A: A is Group 17, a halogen, one place before the noble gas B. Halogens need one electron to complete the octet and share one electron with hydrogen to form covalent HX, for example HCl.
options.B: B is the peak before the large drop, so it is a noble gas in Group 18. Noble gases have a full outer shell and are essentially unreactive, so B will not form HX.
options.C: C is the low point after the large drop, so it is an alkali metal in Group 1. It forms an ionic hydride containing H- ions, not a covalent HX molecule, a common confusion between ionic and covalent hydrides.
options.D: D is one place after C, so it is a Group 2 alkaline earth metal. Group 2 metals form ionic hydrides of formula XH2, such as MgH2, not covalent HX.
